the entropic nature of the chromosome chains and nuclear confinement are the key mechanisms that shape the topological structure of the interphase genome.
the entropic properties of the chromosome arms and nuclear confinement can give rise to the observed topological landscape of the yeast nucleus.

understanding the interplay of physical and biological processes that shape the topological structure of chromosomes.

the entropic nature of the chromosome chains, in combination with the nuclear confinement, is the main driving force of chromosome organization in the cell nucleus, while the biochemical processes are the modulators of the topological landscape.

the topological landscape of the nucleus is a consequence of the entropic interactions of chromosomes and that the role of the nuclear bodies is to modulate this entropic landscape.

chromosomal interactions in interphase nuclei are a result of the interplay between entropic forces, the nuclear environment and the biochemical processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the entropic nature of the chromosomal chains can be the driving force of the formation of topologically associating regions (TADs).
chromatin loops are not required for domain formation, which is in contrast with the current view of the role of loops in shaping chromosomal interactions.
the topological landscape is not an immutable feature of a chromosome, but rather it is a dynamic and flexible property of the chromosomal organization.
